P1.evidence: No setter, so nothing to read back. The four-part frame was never set and no frame agreement was sought — the rep went 'Let's dive into it. If that's okay with you?' straight into 'How did you come across this?'. That is a lead-source question, not the scripted open question; 'ultimately what's really the goal for yourself, Boris?' at 00:02:36 is the nearest equivalent and arrives only after the prospect had already volunteered his situation. The intent of the phase — establish safety, set expectations — did not happen, which matters more than usual on a call where the prospect has a neurological condition and memory impairment.

P2.evidence: The weakest baseline in this batch. Age was never asked — it fell out sideways as 'I'm now 33, not 36' and was never confirmed. Height and current weight were never asked at all; the only body figure on the call is a past best of 85 kg. Work was covered properly ('what kind of engineer were you?', 'what made you leave your job that you were enjoying with the higher pay?'). Health conditions were never asked: multiple sclerosis was volunteered at 00:03:56, which under the spec scores as a miss, and no follow-up was made on treatment, relapse pattern or medical supervision. Injuries were volunteered too, with only 'at what point did you gain full control over your body?' as probing. Diet was volunteered unprompted ('I'm eating clean now, I'm just eating couscous and other high-protein stuff') and never asked about. Sleep, energy and results from current training were not touched.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran well — 'Do you feel like, where you are right now, you're living up to your 100% potential?' produced the engineering and gym regret, and 'How does that pour into the different arenas of your life?' plus the direct 'you're a husband. How does this play out in your relationship with your wife?' surfaced the strongest material on the call: 'Like the weight of the world on my shoulders, man. This sucks. And that's why I need this strength.' But the rep never asked what he wants to do physically and can't, never reflected the goal back in the scripted 'this isn't really about X, it's about Y' form, and — the significant one — never went near the newborn child. The baby was congratulated at 00:01:25 and never raised again. Legacy, fatherhood and being present for a one-month-old are the obvious depth on a call about a degenerative condition, and none of it was used.

P4.evidence: Best-executed phase. 'What is really stopping you from being consistent?' let the prospect name the gap himself — relapses plus short-term memory loss plus training with a trainer he forgets immediately. P4f ran almost verbatim in its intended form: 'what is stopping you from putting together a routine with kettlebells using ChatGPT or YouTube, that is three times a week', which drew out 'I have before, and I see things on ChatGPT, but then I forget that, made that, and then I don't do it.' Past attempts and outcomes were only partially explored — the personal trainer arrangement was never unpacked.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame was run at all. The two-year question, the settle-for question, the 'why not' and the line in the sand were all absent. The rep went directly from root cause to 'so would you like some help to get there?'. The nearest thing was 'is this a now thing for you?' and 'what makes it a now thing', which is an urgency probe rather than a cost-of-inaction frame. This is the phase the call most needed and could most credibly have run: the prospect had already supplied the material himself with 'I don't want to be in bed, not moving' and a history of quadriplegia. Nothing was built on it.

P6.evidence: P6a ran cleanly and got a yes: 'do you ultimately feel like if you had someone guiding you, someone coaching you, someone holding you accountable to show up three times a week, you're going to be able to put that into your long-term memory' — 'Yes.' But the all-in question was never asked, and P6c failed outright. Real hesitation surfaced immediately after the price ('I think I could even do this myself now thinking about it'), and the instruction is to return to Phase 5. The rep instead conceded ground, then downsold to a $200 product. Because Phase 5 had never run in the first place, there was nothing to return to.

P11.evidence: No payment step was reachable. The offer itself was never properly presented — no pillars, no tier structure, no Trevor onboarding call described — so nothing beyond a price range was on the table when the prospect withdrew.

objection_plays.detail: Money was the live blocker from 00:22:00 ('how much would it cost me to get like little videos or snippets?') and the prospect had already signalled cost sensitivity twice — 'that's a lot of money' about his gym and trainer, and the disclosed step down from a ~200k engineering salary to factory work. None of the play ran. No isolation question, no 'you're not in a should-I place, you're in a how place', no 'most clients pay upfront but for some we break it up', and no element of the financial picture — cash, monthly surplus, credit cards, available credit, investments — was asked. Instead the rep opened with an unbounded price range and, on the first sign of resistance, replaced the product with a $200 one.

The call ended on a textbook OA trigger: 'I'll think about it all. Okay, I'll think more in-depthly about this all.' Not one of the seven moves ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. The rep replied 'we're always going to be here' and ended the call.
The wife featured heavily but never as an approval gate — he never said he needed to consult her. She was raised as a substitute for paid accountability, which is a value objection rather than OB.
The prospect affirmed the timing was now; he never deferred on timing.

Cheaper-substitute objection, the known gap in the script, and here in an unusually strong form: the substitute was free and had two components — YouTube plus self-recording for form review, and his wife, a psychologist with 'unbelievable memory', as the accountability layer. The rep half-conceded ('You could do that at the same time'), tried one deserving reframe, and then actively endorsed the substitute: 'as you said, you can use your wife to keep you accountable.' No move existed to defend paid accountability against free accountability that is already in the house.

Clinical-fit gap, the other known hole in the script. The prospect has multiple sclerosis with active relapses, prior quadriplegia and rapid deconditioning. There is no scripted path for establishing whether the programme is appropriate, whether a clinician should be consulted, or how programming adapts around a relapse. The rep improvised a social-proof answer — 'not with MS, but actually maybe one person, but with scoliosis, people with different medical conditions' — which is both weak as persuasion and unsafe as a claim. This is a script gap, not solely a rep failure, and should be logged as one.

notes: Phase 4 was genuinely good and the prospect handed the rep everything needed — a degenerative condition, a newborn, a stated fear of immobility, and an explicit 'I need this strength'. The call was then lost by skipping Phase 5 entirely, never presenting the programme or its actual price structure, and folding to a free substitute inside ninety seconds by downselling to $200. Two coaching priorities: never quote a price range in place of the offer, and when hesitation lands after the number, return to consequence rather than reduce the product. Separately, this call needs a policy answer, not coaching, on how reps handle a disclosed neurological condition.
